tagline: From Lake Ontario through Adirondack communities to twice-Olympic Lake Placid
intro: The Olympic Trail connects Sackets Harbor and Keeseville over 170 miles, from the Lake Ontario region into the Adirondack Mountains. New York’s Department of Transportation identifies scenic and recreational themes for the byway, including places for hiking, camping, canoeing and fishing. Cranberry Lake, Tupper Lake and Saranac Lake lie along the corridor to Lake Placid.

Railways carried both resort passengers and lumber through these mountains. The Delaware and Hudson reached Saranac Lake from Plattsburgh in 1887; five years later, the Mohawk and Malone reached nearby Lake Clear Junction. Lake Placid hosted the Winter Olympics in 1932 and again in 1980.

From Sackets Harbor, the eastward journey reaches Natural Bridge at the western edge of the Adirondacks, then Harrisville. Continue through Star Lake, Cranberry Lake, Tupper Lake and Saranac Lake to Lake Placid and Wilmington, ending at Keeseville. There the Ausable River runs through the community just west of Lake Champlain.

moments.title: Sackets Harbor
moments.text: Navy Point, now a marina for private boats, was the site of a wartime shipyard. During the War of 1812, the U.S. Navy established its Great Lakes headquarters here, and more than 3,000 men worked at the yard. The Army built earthworks, forts and barracks to defend the village and the naval yard. By autumn 1814, Sackets Harbor ranked behind only Albany and New York City among the state’s population centers. The war ended before the last warship, USS New Orleans, was finished. Stored unfinished, she was finally scrapped in 1883. Main Street’s preserved nineteenth-century buildings form part of the village historic district.

moments.title: Natural Bridge
moments.text: The Indian River runs underground through the marble cave that gave Natural Bridge its name. The caverns once operated as a show cave, with visitors taken by boat along the underground river. Joseph Bonaparte, the former king of Spain, built a summer residence here in 1829 after inspecting his land the previous year. That house burned in September 1905, in a fire that also destroyed two hotels, their barns, a store and another house. The hamlet stands on Route 3 at the western edge of the Adirondacks; the Indian River flows north through the community.

moments.title: Saranac Lake
moments.text: Saranac Lake’s cure cottages grew from a doctor’s search for relief from tuberculosis. Edward Livingston Trudeau arrived in 1876 and founded the Adirondack Cottage Sanitarium in 1884, beginning with a cottage called Little Red. Its first patients were two sisters from New York City. Trudeau’s work also led to the Trudeau Institute, an independent research center that began studying the immune system and its defenses against infection in 1964. The architectural legacy includes Marquay Cottage, built in 1914 with a twelve-by-six-foot cure porch. Its walls are rusticated cast-concrete blocks, and an octagonal corner tower carries a pyramidal roof.
